proposals.relationship: Wrigley uses de Vries’s urbanization research and the joint work of de Vries and van der Woude to compare English growth with earlier Dutch development.
proposals.evidence_note: Own Quest (2003), 152–155, notes 12–23, uses European Urbanization (1984) and the JOINT de Vries/van der Woude First Modern Economy (1997) to compare urban growth, occupations, productivity and incomes. Van der Woude retains equal credit. Bairoch, Batou and Chèvre supply a separate 1988 dataset with a different geographical scope (note 13); the calculations are not all de Vries’s alone. This is an empirical and comparative resource, not formal mentorship or independent verification of every figure. The Smithian limits discussed at 157 do not automatically constitute criticism of de Vries.

proposals.relationship: Wrigley uses Mokyr’s two-sector calculation to illustrate why rapid growth in a small modern sector need not produce an immediate surge in aggregate growth.
proposals.evidence_note: Own Quest (2003), 167–168, note 50, explicitly credits Mokyr’s authored editor’s introduction (1993), page 12, in his edited British Industrial Revolution. Wrigley uses the calculation for a somewhat similar purpose: hypothetical modern and traditional sectors initially comprise 10 and 90 percent and grow at 4 and 1 percent; they become equal after 74 years, with aggregate growth then 2.5 percent. This is an illustrative model, not an observed historical estimate, adoption of an entire school, or a fresh reading of Mokyr’s chapter. No independent numerical replication is claimed.
